name: Atlantic croaker
rig: Bottom rig: put a small hook on a short leader, with a sinker above it to hold shrimp near the bottom.
howTo: Cast near the bottom and watch for a light tap. Reel steadily once the line starts moving.
handling: Wet your hands, support the fish, and keep it out of water only briefly. Use pliers to remove the hook.
funFact: Atlantic croaker feed on small fish, worms, crabs, shrimp and shellfish along bay bottoms.

name: Whiting (southern kingfish)
rig: Bottom rig: use a small hook on a short leader with enough weight to hold on the sandy bottom.
howTo: Cast into the surf or from a pier and keep the bait near the bottom. Reel in when the line starts to move.
handling: Wet your hands and support the fish. If releasing it, remove the hook quickly and return it to the water.
funFact: Along the Texas coast, both southern kingfish and Gulf kingfish are called whiting.

name: Sheepshead
rig: Use a small hook and a pinch-on weight. Keep the bait close to pilings, rocks, or other hard surfaces.
howTo: Lower the bait beside structure and watch closely for small bites; sheepshead often nibble before taking it.
handling: Watch the sharp fin spines and gill-cover edge, and keep fingers clear of its strong teeth. Use pliers to unhook it.
funFact: Its human-like front teeth crush barnacles and fiddler crabs; its stripes earned it the nickname “convict fish.”

name: Black drum
rig: Bottom rig: use a circle hook, short leader, and enough weight to hold bait on the bottom.
howTo: Let the bait rest on the bottom near a channel edge or pier. Reel in smoothly when the line moves; avoid jerking hard.
handling: Wet your hands, support the fish under its body, and avoid its gill covers. Keep it in the water when releasing it.
funFact: Young black drum have dark vertical bars that often fade as they grow.

name: Red drum (redfish)
rig: Bottom rig: use a circle hook and sinker to keep shrimp or cut mullet near the bottom.
howTo: Cast near a channel edge or through a moving-water area. Let the bait settle, then reel steadily when the line moves.
handling: Wet your hands and support the fish horizontally. Keep fingers away from its gills and return released fish quickly.
funFact: The dark spot near its tail may fool predators into striking the wrong end.

name: Speckled trout (spotted seatrout)
rig: Popping cork: suspend shrimp or a soft lure below a float. Adjust the leader so the bait hangs above the bottom.
howTo: Cast near moving water, twitch the cork gently, then pause. Watch the float for a pull under.
handling: Wet your hands, support the fish, and keep fingers clear of its teeth. Remove the hook quickly and release it gently.
funFact: Speckled trout belong to the drum family, alongside croaker and red drum.

name: Hardhead catfish
rig: Bottom rig: use a simple hook and sinker to keep bait near the bottom.
howTo: Cast from shore or a pier and wait for the line to move. Check your bait often; catfish may strip it quickly.
handling: Use long-nose pliers or a fish gripper. Never grab the sharp dorsal or side spines; their punctures are painful.
funFact: Its six whisker-like barbels help it find crabs, fish and shrimp.
